articles.title: Red state Republican sticks fork in campaign and gives GOP days to find new candidate
articles.description: State Sen. Mike Bousselot, an Ankeny Republican, announced Friday he is ending his campaign for reelection in Senate District 23 as he “pursues a private-sector professional opportunity.” The Republican Party has until Aug. 19 to nominate another candidate for the 2026 general election ballot. Tony Thompson of Elkhart is the Democratic nominee for the seat. Bousselot will serve until the end of the year when his term ends. “This is not a decision I make lightly,” Bousselot said in a statement. “I am grateful for the opportunity to serve the people of Iowa and humbled by the confidence voters placed in me. It has been a privilege to represent my constituents and participate in the work of the Iowa Legislature.” Bousselot did not specify the professional opportunity but said in his release he had intended to pursue it while continuing to serve in the Iowa Senate. “It was only recently that he learned the requirements associated with the role would not allow him to do both. The position is entirely outside of politics and does not involve lobbying or advocacy before the Iowa Legislature,” the press release stated. Bousselot, 43, was first elected to the Iowa House in a September 2021 special election and then served in the Senate beginning in 2023. He previously served as an adviser to Gov. Terry Branstad, including a stint as chief of staff from 2015 to 2017, and then served in Gov. Kim Reynolds’ administration as director of the Department of Management. In April 2025, he launched an “exploratory” campaign for governor, but withdrew from the race in November.

articles.title: Islamabad bar concerned about Imaan Mazari’s health
articles.description: ISLAMABAD: The Islamabad Bar Association has expressed concerns over the alleged deteriorating medical condition of Imaan Mazari and Hadi Ali Chattha in custody and urged the chief justices of the Islamabad High Court (IHC) and Supreme Court to take immediate notice of the matter. In a letter addressed to the Chief Justice of the Islamabad High Court and the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, IBA Acting President Iram Rashid and Secretary Raja Khawar Dhaniyal highlighted what they described as the serious situation being faced by the two prisoners. According to the letter, Imaan Mazari is suffering from serious medical problems while in jail and requires continuous medical treatment. The bar association stated that Hadi Ali Chattha was also facing a difficult situation and required proper medical attention. The IBA maintained that timely and appropriate medical treatment was a fundamental right of every prisoner and that the authorities concerned were responsible for ensuring that inmates received necessary healthcare facilities. The bar association requested the relevant jail authorities and medical officers to issue immediate instructions for providing continuous and adequate medical treatment to both Imaan Mazari and Hadi Ali Chattha. The IBA also urged the chief justices to fix for early hearing the pending applications seeking suspension of the sentences of the two prisoners. Published in Dawn, August 15th, 2026

articles.title: CNN flags White House's 'remarkable' reaction to Trump's dismissal of suffering sailors
articles.description: The White House had a "remarkable" response to President Donald Trump's response to sailors suffering on the USS Abraham Lincoln. Sailors aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln have been suffering from an ongoing nine-month deployment, which has led to a lack of food and depleted morale. Six sailors are reported to have attempted suicide, and others have jumped ship . Family members of the deployed sailors have attested to the poor conditions, with one slamming Trump. When Trump was asked whether the deployment of the aircraft carrier had gone on too long, he responded, "No, no, no, not nearly long enough." On Friday, CNN White House correspondent Kevin Liptak said White House staff offered no clarification on the comments. "When I went to the White House today to ask if they had any context or wanted to clarify any of the president's comments, they said that they were just going to point back to what the president said, which is really kind of remarkable," Liptak said. "When you talk to people in the military, there is a degree of stunned when you hear what the president said." Liptak noted Trump's reaction to the question. He seemed "visibly irritated" about being asked about the USS Abraham Lincoln. "He kind of snapped after that first answer," Liptak said. "He sort of abruptly turned and walked away, which is not his norm when he's speaking on the tarmac." The USS Abraham Lincoln was deployed ahead of the conflict in Iran. According to Liptak, the attention around the conditions "underscores what is the concern that you hear consistently among American officials, which is just how long this war has gone on." He added, "These lengthy deployments only remind the American public that the president's initial six weeks was absolutely wrong," and noted, "You also hear concerns about the munitions stockpile and the worry that you hear from military officials is that the longer these deployments go on."

articles.title: Trump 'stooge' trolled for wine bar work after Truth Social CEO firing
articles.description: A former GOP lawmaker who abandoned his safe House seat to go to work for President Donald Trump — only to be fired — is now running a wine bar , reports show. In a tongue-in-cheek column for the San Francisco Gate, journalist Anabel Sosa reminded readers that ex-Rep. Devin Nunes (R-CA) was once known as the president's "stooge" during his time in Congress. Jon Fleishman, former California Republican Party, openly cracked jokes about the job shift. “I don’t know what’s better preparation for opening a wine bar, serving in Congress or being a part of the Trump organization,” Fleishman said. “Either of them would wanna make me drink a lot of wine.” Nunes is serving wine in a beachfront community once known as the "Clam Capital of the World" — a plummet from his tenure as CEO of Truth Social where he made $47 million in 2024. He made headlines during the first Trump administration as a Central Valley representative accused of meddling in Trump's Russia investigation to protect the president. He also sued a parody Twitter account called " Devin Nunes' Cow" for $250 million after it called him a "treasonous cowpoke." Nunes left Congress to run Trump's social media platform and has since re-emerged as a wine investor and owner of a new tasting room in Pismo Beach called the Nunes Wine Company. During his time in Congress, Nunes became one of Trump's biggest defenders amid an investigation into whether Russia interfered with the 2016 presidential election. He faced blowback after he was accused of colluding with the White House but was eventually cleared of any wrongdoing by an ethics committee, Sosa wrote. In 2021, Nunes resigned from Congress to become CEO of Trump Media & Technology Group, which owns Truth Social. He left that position in April of this year. .

articles.title: Retail sales slump in July
articles.description: Data: Census Bureau ; Chart: Neil Irwin/Axios American consumers have powered the economy forward this year. In July, they took a breather. Why it matters: While the underlying trend in consumer demand appears solid, retail sales hit an air pocket last month, suggesting a bumpier path ahead for overall growth. Combined with a weak jobs report last week and two subdued inflation readings this week, it points to the Federal Reserve having room to be patient on potential interest rate increases this fall. Driving the news: Retail sales fell 0.6% in July, the weakest performance in more than a year and well below the 0.1% gain analysts expected. Excluding gas stations and auto dealers, there was still a 0.3% decline in sales, meaning that the weakness was evident even apart from those volatile categories. Auto dealers' sales were down 2%, gasoline stations' sales fell 0.9%, and electronic and appliance store sales declined 0.5%. Of note: Some one-off shifts pulled the numbers downward. Amazon held its Prime Day discounting event earlier this year than last, helping explain a 2.2% drop in online sales. Moreover, most World Cup games took place in June, so the associated spending would have the mechanical effect of pushing retail sales upward in early summer and creating a misleading decline in July. Yes, but: The numbers were soft even accounting for those factors, giving some pause as to how robust consumer spending will be in the second half of the year. Growth in Personal Consumption Expenditures contributed a whopping 2.1 percentage points to overall GDP growth in the second quarter, even as other sectors combined to subtract from GDP. The retail sales control group that feeds directly into GDP calculations fell 0.4% in July, versus a 0.3% gain that analysts forecast, and previously reported gains for May and June were revised downward. What they're saying: "The weaker July retail sales report shows that consumers took a breather last month after an ebullient burst of spending in the first half of the year," Nationwide chief economist Kathy Bostjancic wrote in a note. "The contraction in core retail control spending last month, following downward revisions to the prior two months, translates into a bit less momentum for real consumer spending starting Q3 than previously expected." Reality check: The stock market is booming, gasoline prices are well off their recent highs, and the unemployment rate is low. There is no reason to expect broader consumer spending to experience a meaningful pullback. But the July retail numbers suggest there's no major acceleration taking place, either.
